title: The Six-Week Lag: Why Christmas Trading Capital Has to Be Arranged in September, Not November
linkedin:
Six to eight weeks. That's the realistic gap between a business first asking a lender for extra Christmas trading capital and the funds actually landing, once financials, security and internal sign-off are factored in.

Most owner-led retail, hospitality and trade businesses don't feel the squeeze until November, when stock and staffing costs are already loading up and revenue hasn't caught up yet. That's exactly when the finance conversation tends to start.

Apply in November and that six to eight week timeline lands somewhere in the second week of January. Well after the trading peak it was meant to fund.

The businesses that get ahead of this aren't doing anything complicated. They build a short cash flow forecast for the specific peak weeks, check it against what the existing facility can actually absorb, and have the lender conversation while trading is still calm enough to negotiate properly.

An overdraft limit set two Christmases ago was sized for the business as it existed then, not the one trading now. Worth checking before assuming last year's headroom still applies.

Six weeks before the pressure hits is a considered conversation. Six weeks after is damage control.

For retail, hospitality and trade businesses across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria gearing up for the Christmas trading period, now is a good time to check whether your current finance will actually stretch to cover it.

Stock, casual staffing and wages for the busiest six weeks of the year usually fall due well before the season's revenue arrives, and for a lot of owner-led businesses that gap is the single heaviest cash outlay of the year. If extra working capital is needed to bridge it, most Australian lenders take six to eight weeks between a first conversation and funds actually being available, once financials, security and internal approval are factored in. Applied in November, that timeline often lands in January, well after the trading peak it was meant to fund.

The businesses that manage this well aren't doing anything unusual. They build a short cash flow forecast for the specific peak weeks, check it against what their existing facility can actually absorb, and start the lender conversation while trading is still calm enough to negotiate properly rather than scramble later.

If your business hasn't tested its current facility against this year's Christmas trading peak yet, September and early October are the practical window to do it. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
